doc.title: JJ Johnson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Fred Beckett's influence, reissues and early death
summary: The Harlan Leonard Rockets trombonist's records drew trombonists' interest; Johnson recalls his alcoholism and early death.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: After you mentioned that in an interview with somebody, I think virtually every trombone player in the business went to try to find those records.

I think it might have resulted in some of the reissues, because that was the band that Tadd Dameron wrote for – Dameron Swing and Dameron Stomp. Also, that's the band Budd Johnson was playing in. I can't remember the lead alto player's name, but I remember you created a whole interest in Fred Beckett . . .
. . . after you said that he was one of the people who influenced you.

Yeah. He finally went with Lionel Hampton after Harlan Leonard's Rockets. I think there was a band in between, then Lionel Hampton. Then he had a bout with alcoholism – a terrible, terrible bout with alcoholism. It was a tragedy because he was such a talent. He was such a gifted trombonist that it hurt most of us to see him go down with alcoholism. He finally passed away, unfortunately.
Yeah, at a relatively young age.
Thirty or something. [Fred Beckett was 29 when he died.]
He was going to be a force to be reckoned with, no question about it.
Fortunately there are about seven or eight cuts on that album, because that's also the album that had – not 920 Special – I can't remember what the other one
920 Special. Boy. You're bringing back some memories.
